region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Certain Hunting Observances, called |nanna-sse'

summary.en: Hunters eat first the flesh of slow animals, never the springbok's, lest the game they have shot should rise and behave like what they ate; the boy who shot must not touch the meat, for his hands are full of springbok scent; and the springbok possess invisible magic arrows that pierce and fell people who play with its bones.
summary.zh: 獵者先食遲緩獸肉，勿食跳羚肉，免所射之獸起身如所食者而行；射者不得觸肉，因其手滿羚香；跳羚具無形魔箭，戲其骨者立仆。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San ritual instructions dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: When we show respect to the game, we act in this manner; because we wish that the game may die. For the game would not die if we did not show respect to it... a thing which does not run fast is that which we eat, when we have shot game; because we desire that the game should also do as it does.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 271 (public domain).

passages.text: For the game is used to do thus, if we eat the flesh of a thing which is fleet, the thing (i.e. the game) arises; it does like that thing of whose flesh we did eat. Therefore, the old people are accustomed to give us the flesh of a thing which is not fleet. They do not give us all (kinds of) food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 271-272 (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore, the old people fear to give us springbok's meat, because they feel that the gemsbok would not be willing to go to sleep, even at night... The springbok is wont to get into our flesh, and we become ill. And the springbok is inside of us and we become ill on account of it. Therefore, we do not play tricks with springbok's bones.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 272, 277 (public domain).

passages.text: The women do not eat (the meat of) the springbok's shoulder blades, because they show respect for the men's arrows, so that the men may quietly kill... We are wont to be ill when we miss our aim... Therefore, we become ill. The springbok are in possession of (invisible) magic arrows. Therefore, we are ill on account of the springbok.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 277 (public domain).

title.en: Playing the Goura like ||kunh in the Thunderstorm

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Thunderstorm'

summary.en: Rain falling, the boy plays the goura like ||kunh — the rain sorcerer of !khai \ku who, when scolded, held back the rain. His mother rebukes him; he will not listen; and the lightning shivers the stone before the hut. She cries out in pain, says the rain tore her skin, and the boy learns that the rain had meant to kill them for his doings.
summary.zh: 雨落時，童效雨巫古恩（曾憤而止雨者）彈琴。母斥之不聽；雷電碎屋前之石。母痛呼：雷裂我膚。童乃悟：因己所為，雨欲殺其全家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: When the rain fell upon us at night, I did thus, while the rain fell, I lay, playing the 'goura', like ||kun. And mamma said to me, did I not see how the rain was lightening; that I did like ||kun; did I not know that ||kun was a person who used, if people scolded him... to say to the people... that the people seemed to think that the rain would fall; but the rain would stand still, while the rain did not fall.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 321-322 (public domain).

passages.text: When mamma rebuked me, I did not listen to her, for, I lay, playing the 'goura', like ||kun. And mamma became silent... And mamma lay down; I lay, playing the 'goura'. And the rain did thus, as I lay, playing the 'goura', the rain first seemed to shine into our eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 322 (public domain).

passages.text: And the rain lightened, while our eyes felt green. And the rain, lightening, went over us; and the rain did as follows to a stone which stood outside, in front of our hut, the rain, lightening, shivered it. And mamma exclaimed: 'Nnnnn!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 323 (public domain).

passages.text: And mamma told father about it, that the thing seemed as if the rain were tearing off her skin... And mamma said that we had wished to fall dead; it was our fault that we had not been willing to obey her when she rebuked us... I was the one who saw that the rain had intended to kill us, on account of my doings.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 324-325 (public domain).

title.en: The Stone That Burns Bad Dreams

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Mode of getting rid of the evil Influence of Bad Dreams'

summary.en: Before digging, the mother plunges a stone into the fire-ashes crying '\kabbi-a yonder!', so that the evil dreamed of shall stay in the fire and not go out with her; for the Bushman rice knows the dreamer, and would not be favourable to her if she carried the dream.
summary.zh: 掘食前，母將石投入火灰，呼「卡比在那！」，令惡夢留於火中，勿隨身出；因桑人之米知夢者，若攜夢而行，則不賜食。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My mother used to do in this manner, when she intended to go out to seek for food, when she was about to start, she took a stone; and as she plunged the stone into the ashes of the fire, she exclaimed: '\kabbi-a yonder!' while she wished that the evil things, about which she had been dreaming, should altogether remain in the fire; instead of going out with her.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 365 (public domain).

passages.text: That place to which she went would not be nice; while she knew that she had dreamt of evil things which were not nice. Therefore, she acted in this manner; because she was aware that, if she went out with the dream which she had dreamt, her going out would not be fortunate. The Bushman rice which she dug would not be favourable to her, because it was aware that she had dreamt evil things. Therefore, the Bushman rice would act in this manner about it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 365 (public domain).

title.en: Concerning Two Apparitions on the Salt Pan

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Concerning Two Apparitions'

summary.en: Crossing the salt pan after his wife's burial, Dia!kwain's family sees a small child sitting, wearing the cap of his dead wife. \ku-an explains: the sorcerers were taking her away, and what we saw was her outer skin, which still looks at us because she does not want to leave us. A second apparition — a shy child by a bush — frightens a hunter who concludes it is 'a different kind of thing'.
summary.zh: 葬妻後越鹽沼，見幼童坐，戴亡妻之帽。庫安解曰：巫者正攜其去，所見乃其外皮——因不欲離我們而回望。另影：灌木旁畏縮之童，獵者疑為「異物」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal narrative dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: We buried my wife in the afternoon. When we had finished burying her, we returned to the home of my sister, \hai-ttu, and the other people... They had come to bury my wife with me; and we went away, crossing over the salt pan. And we perceived a thing which looked like a little child, as it sat upon the salt pan, seeming as if it sat with its legs crossed over each other.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 366-367 (public domain).

passages.text: \ku-an spoke, she said: 'The old people used to tell me, that the angry people were wont to act thus, at the time when they took a person away, they used to allow the person to be in front of us, (so that) we might see it... she really had a very little child, therefore, ye should allow us to look at the thing which sits upon this salt pan; it strongly resembles a person.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 367 (public domain).

passages.text: For my mothers used to tell me that, when the sorcerers are those who take us away, at the time when they intend to take us quite away, that is the time when our friend is in front of us, while he desires that we may perceive him, because he feels that he still thinks of us. Therefore, his outer skin still looks at us... for he insists upon coming to us.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 368 (public domain).

passages.text: And he examined the child; as the child stood looking at him. He saw that it was a little girl; he saw that the child was like a person. In other parts of it it was not like a person... And he walked on, while the child stood looking from side to side. And the child, when she saw that he went away from it, came forward near the bush, it sat down.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 370-371 (public domain).

title.en: The Jackal's Heart Not to Be Eaten

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Jackal's Heart not to be eaten'

summary.en: A timid child becomes a coward if it eats the jackal's heart; the child eats the leopard's heart instead, which does not fear. Grandfather Tsatsi boils jackals only for his sons, saying: 'Thou dost seem to think that we eat jackals' hearts? for, we become cowards (if we do so).'
summary.zh: 童若食豺心則成懦夫；其當食豹心——豹不畏。祖特薩西煮豺僅予其子，曰：「爾以為吾等食豺心耶？食則懦矣。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San custom dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) feel that a little child is wont to be timid; therefore, the little child does not eat jackals' hearts; because the jackal is not a little afraid; for the jackal runs away. The leopard is the one whose heart the little child eats; it which is not afraid; for, a little child becomes a coward from the jackal's heart, it fears immoderately. Therefore, we do not give to a little child the jackal's heart; because we feel that the jackal is used to run away, when it has not even seen us.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 372 (public domain).

passages.text: Then my grandfather used to act in this manner, when he was boiling a jackal, he said: 'Thou dost seem to think that we eat jackals' hearts? for, we become cowards (if we do so).' Therefore, we did not eat the jackals' hearts. For, my grandfather used not to eat the jackal; he only boiled the jackal for his sons.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 374 (public domain).

title.en: The \tao Mine and the Sorcerers Who Dwell There

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'How \tao is obtained'

summary.en: The red \tao (haematite) lies in a mountain side where sorcerers dwell in mouse-hole houses. Diggers throw stones at the mine so the sorcerers will hide and let them work in peace; and they rub themselves with buchu before going, for they would be ill if the sorcerers saw them.
summary.zh: 赭石\tao藏於山腹，巫者居其間如鼠穴。採者先擲石於礦，令巫躲藏，方得安然掘取；且須先以布庫草擦身，否則被巫見則病。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: \tao is in the mountain, the \tao mine; the people say that the \tao mine is on the side of the mountain... The people are afraid of it, that is, of the sorcerers who live by the mine, because the people are aware that people are there (sorcerers). They (the sorcerers) make a house there.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 379 (public domain).

passages.text: And when they go to the \tao, they throw stones at the \tao mine, when they wish the sorcerers to hide themselves, that they may go undisturbed to work at the \tao, while they feel that the sorcerers dwell at the \tao mine. Therefore, they take up stones, they throw stones at the \tao mine, when they wish the sorcerers to hide themselves. Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's note: they would be ill, if the sorcerers saw them; the \tao mine is also in a different place, and the \hara mine [the black pigment] is in a different place again.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 379 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 380 notes; not verbatim.

title.en: The |xu: Four Pieces of Wood for Divining

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu (!Kung-adjacent) San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The |xu (four pieces of wood used for divining purposes)'

summary.en: The |kun women respect the |xu — four pieces of wood from the \ke tree, two male and two female — and will not touch it; a small girl child is told 'this thing thou must respect'. When the diviner's things fall, the mother asks water for her son; the fall of the |xu speaks, and the beating of the child with a \shana stick ends in the father taking aim at his wife with two arrows.
summary.zh: |昆婦女敬|克烏——\科樹之四木，二男二女——不敢觸之；母戒幼女「此物須敬」。卜者擲之落，其母為子索水；四木落地即言；以夏那枝杖笞子，終致父張弓雙箭向妻。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \kun women respect these things, (they) do not take hold (of them). Men take hold (of them). A small \kun child, who is a little girl, does not take hold of this thing; for (she) respects (it). For, her mother says to her: 'This thing, thou must respect, my mother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 425 (public domain).

passages.text: And the child listens, and respects the thing; but a little male child does not fear the thing, and takes hold of the thing, and carries, carries the thing to his father. And his father puts down the thing upon the ground... For his father objects to his looking on.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 425-426 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The child ran to his mother for water for the divination, dropped the vessel, cried that the water poured out; his father beat him with a \shana stick, the people took hold of the father, and he took aim at his wife with two arrows — one a \nublo and the other a \xu-\ta arrow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 426-428; not verbatim.

title.en: Snakes, Lizards and Small Antelope Near Graves

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'Certain animals, when seen near graves, to be respected'

summary.en: A snake near a grave is our dead person's snake — his spirit; a lizard that walks to our other person's place is followed, not killed; and the little antelope near a grave is not a mere antelope but the spirit antelope of the dead man, with small legs and male. All are respected and left alone.
summary.zh: 墓旁之蛇乃死者之蛇——其靈；蜥行至亡者之地則隨之而不殺；墓旁小羚非尋常羚，乃亡者之靈羚，腿小而為雄。皆敬而任之。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A snake which is near a grave, we do not kill, for, (it) is our other person, our dead person's snake. And we do not kill (it); for (we) respect it. And (if, during) many days, we see it, we do not kill (it); looking (at it), (we) let it alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).

passages.text: Another day, (if) we see a lizard, we follow the lizard's spoor; (if) the lizard has gone to the earth (grave) of our other person, we respect the lizard, (we) do not kill the lizard, (we) let the lizard alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).

passages.text: (When) we see an antelope, an antelope (which is) near our other person's place... we respect the antelope; for, the antelope is not a mere antelope. Its legs seem small, it is the person who has died, and is a spirit antelope. It is a male antelope; it is not a female antelope.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).

title.en: The Snake That Lies Belly-Up to Announce a Death

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'A certain Snake, which, by lying upon its back, announces a death in the family'

summary.en: The \hin, a long pale harmless serpent of the country, turns up its belly to warn of a death in the family; the frightened people go home crying, and tell the household. When it lies normally it may be killed and its skin given to the Makoba; but a snake that shows its belly must never be struck.
summary.zh: 長而色淡無毒之蛇辛，翻腹朝天以示家中將有喪事；眾懼而泣歸，告於家人。若其常臥，則可殺之，皮予馬科巴人；惟翻腹之蛇不可擊。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \hin (is) a serpent of our country. (If, when) we strike it, it does in this manner with its belly, it gives us its belly, we fear it, and go away, and return home; while (we) do not kill it. For (we) let (it) alone; and it lies, lies, lies; arises, and goes away altogether.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 431-432 (public domain).

passages.text: Another day, (when) it sees us, (as) we approach it... (and) it gives us its belly, we are afraid, we do not kill it, we run away. Another day, we see it, (when) it is in the water — tree water — we are near it, we think that we will drink water, we see its body... it quickly goes out of the water, and lies upon the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 432 (public domain).

passages.text: If a woman comes and the woman sees it, (she) unloosens (her) skin necklace, and (gently) lays it down; and it turns, and lays its belly upon the earth. And the woman kills it, and throws it away. (If) another person dies, and we have not heard his news, and we see the \hin turning its belly towards us, we are afraid of the \hin, and cry. And (we) tell the people who are at home, and say: 'I saw a \hin, and struck the \hin; and the \hin objected, and gave me its belly; and I was afraid of the \hin...'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 433 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 433 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: Beating the Ground with a Stone

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Tamme (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'To beat the ground (with a stone)'

summary.en: Only women beat a stone upon the ground, crying 'Fall into the water! Fall into the water!' — and the thing (the lightning) falls into the water. Tamme's father's mother was N-\na; and a man does not do this rite.
summary.zh: 惟婦女擊石於地，呼「落入水中！落入水中！」——雷物遂落於水。塔米之祖母為恩那；男子不行此儀。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Tamme to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \kun beat a stone upon the ground. My father's mother beat a stone upon the ground. She said: 'Fall into the water! Fall into the water!' And the thing (the lightning) fell into the water. A man does not beat a stone upon the ground. A woman beats a stone upon the ground. My (Tamme's) father's mother was N-\na. My mother's father was Little Tamme; and my mother's mother was \karo-\n'a. My father's father's father was Great Tamme.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).

title.en: The Treatment of Thieves Among the |kun

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The Treatment of Thieves'

summary.en: A thieving woman is returned alive to her parents; a woman who returns to steal again is given to the wronged people, who shut her in a hut and burn her — and the husband whose heart aches may kill her with a \nublo arrow. Men thieves are shot with many arrows, not burned; children are only scolded. Those killed are feared for their spirits, and their names are not spoken.
summary.zh: 竊婦活還其親；再犯則交予被害者，閉屋焚之——心痛之夫可以努布羅箭殺之。男賊以群箭射殺，不焚；童賊僅訓斥。被殺者之靈可畏，其名不可言。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; describes capital punishment customs; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: If a \kun woman steals, her father and her mother being (still) there, we take hold of her, we give her to her mother and her father; and they all go away from their place... we say to the other person: 'My wife stole your thing which is here... And I have given back my wife to her father and her mother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 417 (public domain).

passages.text: A female child, if her mother is dead and the female child is an only child, goes to another person's hut. Another day, if she steals, the other person into whose hut she went (to live) takes her, and gives her to the other person (from whom she stole), the other people kill her altogether; (they) put her into a hut, and burn, killing her with fire.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 420 (public domain).

passages.text: They say to the people... they (who) killed the girl... 'We have burning, killed the girl with fire, put the girl into a hut, and burning killed the girl. Leave off reproaching us about the girl.'... 'No; we are not scolding you; for, we object (to stealing)... we hear, and our hearts are glad.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 421 (public domain).

passages.text: If a man steals, we kill (him), we shoot, killing (him) with arrows, and do not put him into the fire; but, kill him altogether with arrows. It is only a woman (whom) we burn... If a child steals, we merely scold the child... Those persons whom we kill altogether, we fear their names; we do not utter their names.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 421 (public domain).
